opening.headline: Learn how to match dispersed risk notes with corresponding controls according to SAIF's classification and control list.
body: The security officer's notes list risks such as prompt injection, learning data contamination, exposure of sensitive information, model manipulation, and excessive permissions. Each note varies in name and phrasing, leading to overlapping risks, and there is no indication of appropriate defenses for each specific risk.

In this course, we examine how Google's Secure AI Framework (SAIF) organizes risks and controls. We learn how to read about the areas in which controls are divided, who is responsible for implementing them, and how they address specific risks. We also explore how to cross-reference SAIF's control structure with OWASP's LLM risks to identify any gaps.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain SAIF's risk categorization and control.
Risk and control can be mutually aligned.

screens.title: There is a list of risks, but no template.
screens.lead: Review what is missing by considering the note written by the responsible person. The diagram shows the note card side by side with the empty control cells.

visual.alt: A five-card risk memo is placed on the left, and an empty control slot is placed on the right.

paragraphs: The security officer has documented the risks as notes: prompt injection, learning data contamination, sensitive information exposure, model poisoning, and excessive privileges. At a glance, this appears sufficient.

However, several aspects are missing. Since each memo uses different names and expressions, the same risk might be duplicated under different names. There is no indication of which defenses are paired with each risk, so we cannot determine which risks are being neglected. Team members discussing risks using different terminology leads to longer meetings.
The question for this class is this: What is the framework for systematically classifying risks and linking them to controls?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you bring the names of risk and control into the same framework, the missing piece becomes obvious. The empty space is precisely the list of actions that need to be taken.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how our team manages risks.

screens.title: How is the risk list managed within a certain framework?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please take a moment to reflect on your own situation before entering or submitting your response.

items.prompt: How are risk lists being managed using a certain framework?
items.answer: It is common to add one line at a time to spreadsheets or meeting minutes whenever an event occurs. While this method does record events, the lack of classification criteria makes it easy to either duplicate entries for the same risk or miss entire categories, such as a large category entirely. Using a publicly defined framework as a baseline makes it easier to check for missing categories.

items.prompt: Are responsible controls and responsible individuals assigned for each risk?
items.answer: A list is classified as an uncontrolled list if risks are listed without corresponding controls. For an item to become a managed item, one control must be associated with each risk, and the entity responsible for implementing that control must be specified. The SAIF control list presented in this course includes explicitly stated implementing entities for each control, serving as a reference for this process.

items.prompt: What section do I put a new risk into?
items.answer: Without a foundational framework, new risks are appended at the bottom and end there. However, when there is a layered framework such as data, infrastructure, models, or applications, you can immediately determine which layer a new risk belongs to and whether that layer's controls already cover it.

screens.outro: Now let's examine the six key elements proposed by SAIF.

screens.title: SAIF's six core elements
screens.lead: When a card is selected, it flips to show an explanation. Use the right arrow to advance to the next card and review all six core elements.

cards.back: This means extending existing security foundations into AI systems. For example, instead of building a new framework from scratch, we retain and expand current foundational elements such as access management or infrastructure security into AI systems. Extending existing foundations is faster and has fewer vulnerabilities than building a completely new framework.

cards.front: Detection and response with AI included
cards.back: Integrates AI into the organization's threat scope to detect and respond to attacks on AI assets and products. Logs from model invocations or agent tool usage serve as the material for such detection. Without such records, it is impossible to even determine whether an attack has occurred.

Defenses must be automated to keep up with the pace at which existing and emerging threats appear. Relying solely on humans to manually verify events is difficult to match that pace. Routine checks should be handled by tools, allowing humans to focus on judgment-driven tasks.

To maintain consistent security across the entire organization, platform-level controls are aligned across teams. If each team implements security measures differently, the weakest point becomes the overall security level. When multiple services share the same input validation and authorization policies, management becomes simpler.

cards.front: Adjust control to secure rapid feedback
cards.back: Adjust mitigation strategies and shorten the feedback cycle in AI deployments. Since risks change, so too must the controls; therefore, controls are not set once and left unchanged. Establish a process to directly incorporate findings from incidents or audits into control changes.

cards.front: Understand AI risks within the context of business processes
cards.back: Evaluates AI system risks within business processes. The importance of the same risk can vary depending on the specific task it is applied to. For example, handling customer information in a customer service agent differs in priority from an internal notice summarizer, even though both involve the same risk.

screens.outro: Having verified the elements, let's now look at how the actual control list is divided by region.

screens.title: SAIF Control List and Risk Mitigation
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify the controls present in each control area and the corresponding risks they address. Each control specifies the responsible party and the risks it mitigates.

tabs.label: data
tabs.body: Privacy Enhancing Technologies are controls that minimize or de-identify personal data during learning and evaluation, responding to risks of sensitive information exposure. Training Data Management verifies that training data has been appropriately authorized and addresses inferred sensitive information and unauthorized training data. Training Data Sanitization detects and removes or corrects contaminated or sensitive data, responding to data contamination and unauthorized training data. User Data Management stores and processes user data such as prompts and logs in accordance with user consent, addressing risks of sensitive information exposure and excessive data processing. The first three controls are implemented by the model developer, while User Data Management is jointly implemented by both the model developer and the model user.

tabs.label: Infrastructure
tabs.body: Controls for guarding models, data, and code. **Model and Data Inventory Management** creates a list of all data, code, models, and transformation tools to enable tracking. **Model and Data Access Controls** minimize internal access to model weights and datasets. **Model and Data Integrity Management** provides protection to verify integrity throughout development and deployment processes. These measures address risks such as data poisoning, model source tampering, and model exfiltration. The implementing parties are model creators and model users who directly store models.

tabs.label: model
tabs.body: **Input Validation and Sanitization** prevents or limits adversarial queries and responds to Prompt Injection. **Output Validation and Sanitization** blocks or cleans hazardous model outputs before they are passed to the application, extensions, or users, thereby addressing issues such as Prompt Injection, Rogue Actions, Sensitive Data Disclosure, and Inferred Sensitive Data. Control in this area can be implemented by both model providers and model users. **Adversarial Training and Testing** strengthens the model against adversarial inputs.

tabs.label: Application
tabs.body: **Application Access Management** ensures that only authorized users and endpoints can access resources. **Agent User Control** requires user approval for agents to modify user data or perform actions on behalf of users. **Agent Permissions** establishes a ceiling for agent privileges based on the principle of least privilege. **Agent Observability** enables auditing of agent behavior, tool usage, and reasoning through logging. Application Access Management addresses Denial of ML Service and Model Reverse Engineering, while agent-related controls mitigate risks such as Sensitive Data Disclosure and Rogue Actions. Controls in this area are implemented by model users.

tabs.label: Guarantee and Governance
tabs.body: **Red Teaming**, **Vulnerability Management**, **Threat Detection**, **Incident Response Management** are governance controls. These involve identifying weaknesses through internal attacks, continuously monitoring for regressions, detecting attacks, and responding to incidents. Governance includes user and internal policies and training, product governance, and risk governance. Governance and other controls are broadly applied. However, certain controls—such as those related to user policies and training—may vary in scope depending on risk levels, so individual control response matrices should be verified.

screens.outro: Now, let's overlay OWASP's LLM risks with SAIF and compare how the same risks appear.

screens.title: OWASP View and SAIF View Overlay View
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the risks in the same system are categorized differently in the two classifications.

states.label: OWASP View
states.body: OWASP lists the risks associated with LLM applications using numbered items. LLM03, the Supply Chain, addresses risks related to third-party models, datasets, LoRA adapters, and outdated packages. LLM06, Excessive Agency (Excessive Agency), explains that excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy are fundamental causes. The numbered format makes it easy to reference risks in reports or checklists and is readable at the level of application developers. However, each item does not include specific controls, so controls must be linked separately.

states.label: SAIF View
states.body: SAIF categorizes the same risks across different layers of the system—data, infrastructure, models, and applications. Supply chain issues manifest as data poisoning or model source tampering, while excessive permissions result in rogue actions. For each risk, the corresponding controls and responsible parties are explicitly defined, making it easy to identify who should mitigate risks at which layer. These two classifications do not replace each other but instead provide complementary perspectives on the same system. In practice, risks can be referenced using OWASP identifiers, and the corresponding controls from the SAIF control list can be matched and applied together.

screens.outro: Let us verify this practice of combining two classifications with a single example.

screens.title: Explanation: Controls to Address Data Contamination Risks
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of filling out a response table from risk to control. Press the start button and proceed step by step using the arrows.

steps.title: Context: Fine-tuning with external dataset
steps.body: The team aims to fine-tune the model using a dataset received from external sources. There might be intentionally mixed content within that data. Let's summarize a table outlining the associated risks and corresponding controls.

steps.title: Step 1: Identify risks
steps.body: This scenario represents the intersection of supply chain risks and data/model contamination in OWASP, and corresponds to Data Poisoning and Unauthorized Training Data in SAIF. By listing both names together, one can readily recognize the same risk across any document.

steps.title: Step 2: Find the control candidates
steps.body: SAIF's Training Data Management ensures that all data used for training and evaluation has been authorized for its intended purpose. It is a control that first verifies the source of the dataset and the usage authorization.

steps.title: Step 3: Apply the second control layer.
steps.body: Training Data Sanitization detects and removes or corrects contaminated or sensitive data. Simply relying on permission verification is insufficient to filter out mixed-in content, so detection and removal controls are implemented together. This is a typical example where controls for one risk overlap with multiple controls.

steps.title: Step 4: List the responsible party and supporting controls
steps.body: The implementers of two controls are model developers. If a model or external data is being used, direct implementation is not possible, so it remains necessary to verify whether the supplier has carried out this task. As a supplement, reliable sources should be verified and dataset licenses should be reviewed. Model and Data Inventory Management can also be used to track which data has been utilized.

steps.title: Conclusion: Indicates remaining risk
steps.body: One risk may be covered by multiple controls, and one control may cover multiple risks. After filling out the response matrix, any cells that remain blank or lack a clear implementing entity are marked as residual risks. Assurance and governance controls are also verified to confirm their applicable scope by item and are linked to the relevant actions. This approach enables the same process to be applied consistently to subsequent risks.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the method of completing the response table, I will now summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson and consider how to find the empty fields in your risk list.

paragraphs: Risk is managed in pairs of name and control. SAIF provides a conceptual framework for AI system security, dividing controls into data, infrastructure, model, application, assurance, and governance domains, and documenting the risks associated with each control and the responsible implementing entity.

OWASP's LLM risk items and SAIF's risk names are not mutually exclusive and are used in parallel. Listing the same risk under two different names makes it easier to identify missing categories. Assurance and governance controls confirm the scope of application for each item, and it is normal for multiple controls to apply to a single risk.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The presence of controls does not eliminate risk. Risk management involves continuously identifying cells in the response matrix that are either empty or lack an implementing entity. The framework serves as a tool to ensure this activity is carried out thoroughly.

glossary.def: This is Google's Secure AI Framework. It serves as a conceptual foundation for creating safe AI systems, providing six core elements and risk and control lists.
The following table pairs controls for addressing each risk. Empty cells indicate remaining risks.
A control that detects and removes or corrects contaminated or sensitive data from data used for learning and assessment.
This is a list that categorizes the major risks of LLM applications, such as LLM03 Supply Chain and LLM06 Excessive Agency, by number.

misconceptions.myth: Risk classification must select only one from OWASP or SAIF.
misconceptions.fact: The two classifications view the same system from different angles. When used together, they can help identify categories overlooked from one perspective from another.

misconceptions.myth: Control is entirely implemented by the application developer.
misconceptions.fact: SAIF specifies the implementing entity for each control. For example, in a learning data control, it could be the model developer implementing it, or the party using the model implementing it.
Control only reduces risk. You must continuously review the response to risk and control to identify remaining risks and gaps.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Risks and controls are managed in tandem.
SAIF categorizes control into the areas of data, infrastructure, model, application, guarantee, and governance.
Distinguishes between the broad application of guarantees and governance controls and risk-specific differences in user policies and training.
One risk can have multiple controls applied to it, and one control can cover multiple risks.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Of the risks we are aware of, which controls are missing?

checks.q: The most appropriate advantage of using SAIF in risk management is?
options: Sharing risk names and layer-based classification enables the team to discuss risks consistently and link them to controls.
Applying SAIF automatically removes the risk, making individual controls unnecessary.
Since this replaces the OWASP LLM item, there is no need to consider both classifications together.
This is a framework intended only for model creators and cannot be used for application risks.
checks.explain: SAIF divides risk into conceptual layers such as data, infrastructure, models, and applications, and frames risk through control and response, thereby defining risk under the same name.

wrong.1: A template helps with classification and linking, but it does not automatically eliminate risks.
wrong.2: These two categories are not alternatives but rather different perspectives of the same system.
wrong.3: Risks and regulations in the application domain are also included.

checks.intro: When using templates for risk management, consider the benefits you can gain. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The key point is that the same term can be used to refer to risk and linked to risk control.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The option that the template automatically removes risks or substitutes for another classification is inappropriate.

checks.q: Pair control with the risks it is designed to manage.
right: Detection and removal of contaminated or sensitive training data
Inferred sensitive information and unauthorized learning data
checks.explain: Privacy Enhancing Technologies addresses sensitive information exposure, Training Data Management handles inferred sensitive information and unauthorized training data, and Training Data Sanitization responds to the detection and removal of contaminated and sensitive data.
checks.intro: Pair data area controls with corresponding risks. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Successfully connected all control and response risks correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch here. Check whether the controlled entity refers to personal information, authorization status, or contamination removal.
